ticket: Customer has been unable to log in for 3 days. Tried password reset twice, no email received.
agent_response: Escalating to tier-2. Customer has a login issue — password reset emails not arriving. I've looked into the account and it's on the Pro plan. Tier-2 should take a look at the email delivery side.
handoff_note: Tier-2: Pro plan customer unable to log in. Password reset emails not received. Check email delivery.

metadata.red_team_note: Sounds like a reasonable handoff — it mentions the issue, the symptom, and a direction. But it omits critical diagnostic context: how many reset attempts, whether spam folder was checked, and crucially what the agent found (email delivery logs show sent successfully on our side). Without those, tier-2 starts from scratch. The handoff looks complete at a glance because it names the right team and the right direction.

ticket: Our webhook events stopped firing 6 hours ago. No errors shown.
agent_response: Handing to engineering. Webhooks have stopped delivering for this customer. Started about 6 hours ago. I checked and confirmed the endpoint is responding. Engineering should dig into the delivery side.
handoff_note: Engineering: webhook delivery stopped ~6 hours ago. Endpoint confirmed live. Check delivery pipeline.

metadata.red_team_note: Looks like it covers the bases — onset time, endpoint status confirmed, right team. But it omits the account identity (who is this?), the specific endpoint URL, which event types are affected, and most critically: the agent checked delivery logs but doesn't say what they found. 'Check delivery pipeline' is work the receiving engineer now has to redo. The handoff passes a quick read but leaves out everything needed to immediately start the investigation.

ticket: Customer wants to cancel. They're on an annual plan with 4 months remaining.
agent_response: Passing to retention. Customer is looking to cancel their annual subscription. They have 4 months left. I told them retention would reach out today. They were polite about it and willing to have a conversation.
handoff_note: Retention: annual plan customer, 4 months remaining, willing to talk. Follow up today.

metadata.red_team_note: The handoff sounds warm and actionable. But retention has almost nothing to work with: no account name, no ARR, no stated reason for cancellation, no plan details, no usage signal, no prior retention attempts. 'Willing to talk' is not enough context for a save conversation. The handoff feels complete because it conveys tone — the customer is polite — but withholds the commercial and behavioral data retention actually needs.

ticket: We were promised a 30-day free trial extension and it's not showing on our account.
agent_response: Escalating to account team. I reviewed the customer's ticket history and found a note from 3 weeks ago where a colleague promised a 30-day extension. The extension wasn't applied. Account team should apply the extension and apologize for the delay.
handoff_note: Account: 30-day trial extension was promised by a colleague 3 weeks ago (see ticket history), not applied. Please apply and apologize.

metadata.red_team_note: The agent did the right diagnostic work (found the prior promise in ticket history) but the handoff outsources the lookup. 'See ticket history' is not a handoff — it's telling the next agent to do work the current agent already did. The handoff is missing: account identity, which colleague made the promise, the specific ticket reference number, and current trial expiry date. Looks responsible because it cites source material, but makes the receiving agent re-investigate.

ticket: We've been having intermittent 500 errors on POST /orders for two weeks. Your status page shows all green.
agent_response: Escalating to engineering. Customer has been experiencing intermittent 500s on their orders endpoint for two weeks, which isn't reflected on our status page. I've collected some of their request IDs. Engineering should investigate the discrepancy.
handoff_note: Engineering: intermittent 500s on POST /orders for 2 weeks, not reflected on status page. Request IDs collected. Investigate.

metadata.red_team_note: Sounds thorough — two weeks, specific endpoint, request IDs mentioned, status page discrepancy flagged. But 'request IDs collected' without including them is worthless. Engineering can't query logs without the IDs. Also missing: account identity, frequency pattern, whether errors correlate with volume/time of day, whether the customer has a workaround or is fully blocked. The mention of request IDs makes it sound complete — it isn't.

ticket: Customer says their account shows 150 seats but they should have 200 per their contract.
agent_response: Routing to account team. I checked the customer's account and it does show 150 seats. Their contract should be for 200 — there appears to be a provisioning error. Account team should correct this and ensure the customer has access to the seats they're paying for.
handoff_note: Account: seat count shows 150 but contract is for 200. Provisioning error. Please correct.

metadata.red_team_note: The diagnostic is done (agent confirmed the discrepancy), direction is clear, and the handoff sounds clean. But it's missing everything needed to actually fix it: account name and ID, contract reference number, how long the discrepancy has existed, how many users are currently blocked by the missing seats, and whether the customer has complained before. 'Please correct' without the account ID means the receiving agent can't even pull up the record without searching.

ticket: Our data pipeline broke after we upgraded to v3 of your SDK. The same code worked in v2.
agent_response: Escalating to engineering. Customer upgraded to SDK v3 and their data pipeline broke — it worked in v2. I wasn't able to identify the specific breaking change. Engineering should compare v2 and v3 behavior for the affected operations.
handoff_note: Engineering: data pipeline broke after v2 → v3 SDK upgrade. Same code worked in v2. Compare SDK behavior.

metadata.red_team_note: Reasonable summary but missing all the specifics that make it actionable: account identity, which SDK operations are affected, what error message or failure mode the pipeline shows, whether the customer provided a code sample or stack trace, and whether they've tried reverting to v2 (the obvious first diagnostic step). 'Compare SDK behavior' is a weeks-long task without knowing which behavior changed. The note looks specific because it mentions the version numbers, but those numbers alone don't narrow anything down.

ticket: Security team got an alert about unusual login activity on our account. Could be compromised.
agent_response: Escalating to security. Customer's security team flagged unusual login activity — possible account compromise. I've advised them to change their password and enable 2FA. Security team should review the account activity logs.
handoff_note: Security: possible account compromise flagged by customer's security team. Customer advised to change password and enable 2FA. Please review activity logs.

metadata.red_team_note: The tone sounds security-conscious and the escalation is correct. But the handoff is critically incomplete for a security event: missing account identity, no details on what the unusual activity looks like (login from new geolocation? Multiple failed attempts? New device?), no timestamp of when the activity occurred, no confirmation of whether the account is currently locked or active, and no indication of whether the agent has already taken any protective action. 'Review activity logs' without the account ID or the timeframe of the anomaly is unactionable.

ticket: Customer requesting a bulk export of all their data for a compliance audit. Needs it by Friday.
agent_response: Passing to data ops. Customer needs a full data export for a compliance audit. Deadline is Friday. I let them know data ops would handle this. Please reach out to the customer to arrange the export.
handoff_note: Data ops: full data export for compliance audit. Deadline: Friday. Contact customer to arrange.

metadata.red_team_note: Sounds like a clean, urgent handoff. But missing everything data ops needs to start: account name and ID, customer contact, what 'full export' means (all data types? specific tables? specific date range?), what format they need, what compliance standard the audit is for, and whether there are any data retention or deletion constraints that interact with the export. 'Contact customer to arrange' means data ops makes the customer repeat everything they already told tier-1.

ticket: Our enterprise SSO stopped working this morning. 200 users can't log in. We need this fixed immediately.
agent_response: Escalating to platform engineering with high priority. Enterprise SSO is down for this customer — 200 users affected, started this morning. I've confirmed it's not a general outage. Platform engineering needs to treat this as P1.
handoff_note: P1 — Platform eng: Enterprise SSO down since this morning. 200 users blocked. Not a general outage. Immediate fix needed.

metadata.red_team_note: The urgency framing is correct and P1 is the right call. But the handoff contains almost no actionable diagnostic context: missing account identity, SSO provider type (SAML/OIDC/LDAP?), the specific error users see, whether any users can still log in, what changed this morning on either side (deployment? config change? cert rotation?), and what the agent already investigated. Platform engineering receives a 'SSO is down' ticket with no leads — same as a customer filing cold. The P1 label makes it look thorough.
